summary:
FireBridge is a web tool that makes MODIS and VIIRS fire detections comparable, so one continuous fire record can be built from both sensors. It is a FastAPI and DuckDB backend with a React and MapLibre map interface.
Users upload NASA FIRMS archive or NRT files, as CSV or ZIP, or import them with a FIRMS key. FireBridge reads the files from any region of the world. It normalizes the differences between Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. These include satellite codes, brightness channels, confidence classes, and archive versus near-real-time processing. It then places every detection on a common grid, removes exact duplicates, and fits a harmonization model from the period when the sensors overlap. The map shows the results, and every import keeps an audit record of columns, platforms, dates and rows processed.
This addresses the challenge directly. MODIS and VIIRS have different resolution, overpass times and detection sensitivity, so their raw hot spot counts cannot simply be added together or compared.
It matters because fire trends, emissions estimates and risk maps depend on long records. MODIS is aging and VIIRS is taking over, so those records need a documented way to bridge the two sensors.
details:
FireBridge: project details
What it does and how it works
FireBridge harmonizes active fire detections from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) so they can be analysed as one record.
Ingest. The user uploads NASA FIRMS archive or near-real-time files (CSV or ZIP, several at once) or imports them with a FIRMS key. The tool reads data for any region of the world. It checks the files, reports what is wrong with a bad file, and recognises the same file if it is uploaded twice.
Normalize. It maps the sensors’ different conventions onto one schema: satellite codes, MODIS and VIIRS brightness channels, confidence values and classes, day/night flags, and archive versus NRT processing. It applies a quality filter and keeps an audit record of columns, platforms, dates and row counts for every file.
Harmonize. Detections go onto a common grid, and exact duplicates are removed with archive data preferred over NRT. A harmonization model is fitted on the period when the sensors overlap, so counts from one sensor can be compared with the other. The model is marked stale when new data arrives.
Explore. A MapLibre map shows the harmonized activity by sensor, date and region.
Benefits
One comparable fire record across the MODIS-to-VIIRS transition, instead of a break in the series.
Every step is documented, so a user can see how each number was produced.
Researchers can load their own FIRMS downloads without writing code.
It runs on a free-tier server (512 MB of memory) and also on a laptop.
Intended impact
Fire trends, emissions estimates, risk maps and seasonal reports all rely on long records. MODIS is aging and VIIRS is taking over, so a documented way to bridge the two helps keep those records consistent. We want that to be usable by non-programmers such as local agencies, students and journalists.
Tools, languages and software
Backend: Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, pandas, pydantic.
Frontend: React, MapLibre GL, JavaScript.
Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS active fire products).
Deployment: Render, GitHub.
Testing: pytest and Playwright (a real browser) for the ZIP upload.
AI tools: Claude (Anthropic) helped with coding, testing and the pitch deck.
Hardware: ordinary laptops and a free cloud instance, with no special hardware.
What is creative
It treats harmonization as a data-engineering and audit problem rather than only a statistical one: the same tool that corrects the counts also explains where each number came from.
The user can drag in a ZIP from FIRMS and see a harmonized map. Usually this takes a custom script.
Memory limits adjust automatically to the server, so the same code works on a small free instance and on a local machine.
What we considered
Sensor differences: resolution, overpass time, sensitivity and confidence definitions are not the same across MODIS and VIIRS.
Duplicates and processing versions: archive data should replace NRT data for the same detection.
Reproducibility: idempotent imports and audit records.
Failure cases: broken ZIPs, wrong formats and oversized files get clear messages instead of silent errors.
Resource limits: large archives on a small server, and the fact that a free server loses its data when it restarts. For that reason the live demo uses a smaller data set, and larger runs are done locally.
Scope: the tool is global, not tied to one country.
Before submitting, check the sentence about the harmonization model against what your team actually implemented, and add real numbers (for example, rows processed or the overlap period) if you have them.
